strengths: Originality: Extending error-feedback analysis to TD learning provides useful theoretical understanding. The treatment of coupled parameter, memory, and Markov sampling dynamics is a substantive contribution beyond simply proposing a compressed update.

Significance: Theorem 5 separates a leading statistical term scaling as 1/(MT) from a higher-order compression term. This is a useful result for distributed policy evaluation under the stated homogeneous, i.i.d. sampling assumptions.

Presentation: The progression from deterministic to stochastic and multi-agent settings is clear. Algorithms 1–2, proof sketches, and extensive appendices make the approach inspectable. Figure 2 provides an informative error-feedback ablation.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript openly acknowledges the projection requirement, unresolved compression dependence under Markov sampling, and restricted multi-agent sampling model. These disclosures are appropriate. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent in the theoretical work and synthetic experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—advertised compressor: Sections 1 and 3 describe replacing each coordinate by its sign, but this operator does not satisfy Eq. (4). For scalar x=0.1, the squared compression error is 0.81, whereas the right-hand side is below 0.01 for every finite δ. A suitably scaled sign operator can satisfy the assumption, but its scaling and implementation must be specified. Consequently, the theory does not currently cover SignTD as described, including its connection to the experiments.

Soundness—nonlinear theorem: Theorem 4 refers to unprojected Algorithm 1 and requires only αβ<1, while Appendix F relies on the projected recursion and bounded iterates. The unprojected statement is false: take deterministic g(θ)=(-I+10J)θ, where J is a 90-degree rotation. This satisfies the assumptions with β=1 and L=√101, but α=1/2 makes the squared iterate norm grow by a factor of 25.25 each step. The theorem must explicitly require projection or provide sufficient stability conditions and an appropriate unprojected proof.

Proof accuracy: Lemma 4 incorrectly asserts a unit Lipschitz bound. With P=[[0.1,0.9],[0.9,0.1]], feature vector (1,-1), and γ=0.9, Σ=1 but the mean TD matrix is -1.72, contradicting both the Lipschitz claim and the asserted matrix inequality. Also, the choice η=δ-1 in Lemma 6 gives a coefficient of 1, not 1-1/(2δ). These appear repairable, but the dependent inequalities and constants require correction.

Significance and scope: The compression-independent leading term is an asymptotic statement whose useful regime needs clarification. Comparing the terms in Eq. (12), the compression term becomes smaller only when T substantially exceeds δ²M/[ω(1-γ)²], ignoring logarithms. For top-1 compression, δ=K, so this transient can be substantial. The description that communication efficiency comes 'almost for free' overstates the demonstrated finite-time benefit.

Communication accounting: Top-1 transmits an index and a real-valued magnitude; the manuscript does not specify the precision needed to justify its bit count. Algorithm 2 also broadcasts the full K-dimensional model every round. The claimed O~(1)-bit communication should be qualified as an uplink claim under an explicit precision convention, rather than presented as a complete communication guarantee.

Reproducibility and evaluation: Section 8 omits experimental step sizes, precise transition/feature generation procedures, initialization details, and compressor scaling, and supplies no code link or uncertainty estimates. Figures 4–5 demonstrate lower error floors with more agents, but do not directly test the weighted-iterate rate of Theorem 5 or communication to a target accuracy. The simulations are useful illustrations, but cannot resolve the technical mismatches above.
